```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%")
library(SMSD)
study <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "coverage_study.rds", package = "SMSD"))
results <- study$summary
trials <- study$trials
reference <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "normal_reference.rds",
                                 package = "SMSD"))
stopifnot(all(results$G >= 1000), all(results$conf_level == 0.95))
```

## What Does a Satisfied Rule Mean?

The AIPE stopping rules ensure that the reported confidence interval is
no wider than the requested target. Coverage relies on asymptotic
approximations under the relevant regularity conditions:
at the sample size where a particular study stops, the probability that
the interval contains the population value can be much smaller. A narrow
interval can miss its target very consistently.

This vignette follows two difficult settings identified in a package
quality review: a strong Pearson correlation and a multiple correlation
with many predictors. All simulated results come from completed studies,
rather than expected sample size formulas. The separate null-boundary
calculation below uses the exact fixed sample distribution. No simulation
is run while this vignette is built.

## Where These Intervals Come From

The Pearson procedure uses the stopping rule and interval in Kelley,
Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019), Equations 10 and 11, with the moment
variance estimator in Equation 70. The multiple R-squared procedure uses
the Wald interval in Equation 59, based on the normal approximation of
Olkin and Finn (1995), and the stopping rule corresponding to Equation 63.
The help page `?seq_aipe_R2` explains the correction to the printed stopping
formula used to reproduce the published tables.

These are specific stress tests. The article's multiple R-squared tables
use 2, 5, and 10 predictors, positive population values, and widths of
0.05 and 0.10. Twenty predictors at a population value of zero extend
beyond those conditions. A Pearson width of 0.4 also permits a very small
pilot. Performance in these settings should be distinguished from
performance in the published simulation designs.

## Design and Reproducibility

Each condition has `r unique(results$G)` independent studies, a nominal
confidence level of 95%, and multivariate normal observations. The
Pearson population correlation is 0.8. For multiple R-squared, predictors
are independent standard normal variables and the response has variance
one, with equal predictor coefficients and independent normal error.
The population R-squared is either 0 or 0.5.

A study begins at the pilot size returned by the matching package
function. It checks the exported stopping rule after each additional
observation, stopping the first time that rule is met. The largest
allowed sample is 5,000. The table reports any studies that reached that
limit without stopping. The larger pilots and narrower widths are
comparisons to evaluate, not general prescriptions for adequate coverage.

```{r designs}
knitr::kable(results[, c("id", "procedure", "truth", "p", "width",
                        "m_0", "pilot")],
             col.names = c("ID", "Procedure", "Population value", "Predictors",
                           "Target width", "Minimum pilot", "Actual pilot"),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

The generating script is `data-raw/coverage_study.R` in the source
repository. It saves every study's sample size, estimate, limits,
coverage indicator, width, and stopping status, along with the software
version, seeds, and function fingerprints. The full data are installed
with the package:

```{r inspect-data}
names(study)
head(trials)
study$meta[c("generated_on", "package_version", "R", "generator")]
```

## Actual Coverage and Its Monte Carlo Uncertainty

Coverage is the fraction of studies whose final interval includes the
known population value. Its Monte Carlo standard error describes
uncertainty from the finite number of simulated studies. The plotted
95% intervals are exact binomial intervals for that simulation
probability. They are not confidence intervals for the population
correlation or R-squared in an individual study.

```{r actual-results}
table <- results[, c("id", "coverage", "coverage_mcse", "coverage_lower",
                     "coverage_upper", "pct_width_within", "pct_capped")]
knitr::kable(table, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("ID", "Coverage", "MC SE", "MC lower", "MC upper",
                           "% within width", "% capped"))
```

```{r coverage-plot, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Coverage by simulated design with exact binomial uncertainty intervals and a reference line at the nominal 95 percent level. Labels state the procedure, population value, target width, and actual pilot size."}
labels <- sprintf("%s: value %g, w=%g, pilot=%d",
                   ifelse(results$procedure == "Pearson", "Pearson",
                           paste0("R-squared (p=", results$p, ")")),
                   results$truth, results$width, results$pilot)
position <- rev(seq_len(nrow(results)))
par(mar = c(4, 21, 2, 1))
color <- ifelse(results$procedure == "Pearson", "#176B87", "#955019")
plot(results$coverage, position, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0.5, nrow(results) + 0.5),
      pch = 19, col = color, yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
      xlab = "Empirical coverage")
axis(2, at = position, labels = labels, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.75)
segments(results$coverage_lower, position, results$coverage_upper, position,
          col = color, lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0.95, lty = 2, col = "#555555")
legend("bottomright", "Nominal 95%", lty = 2, bg = "white",
        box.col = "white", cex = 0.85)
```

The two conditions that reproduce the review's concern are the first and
fifth rows. In this new run the Pearson design covered in
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * results$coverage[1])` of studies, and the
20-predictor null R-squared design covered in
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * results$coverage[5])`. A separate earlier
review with 1,000 studies found 67.4% and 2.9%, respectively. The seeds and
random streams differ; both runs show coverage far below its nominal level.

## What Happens in Individual Studies?

The next figure shows the first 60 independent studies in each baseline
condition, in their original order. Blue intervals include the population
value; orange intervals miss it. These are the intervals produced at
the actual stopping points. The dashed line marks the population value.

```{r interval-plot, fig.height=5, fig.alt="Final intervals from the first 60 baseline studies. Most intervals for the null multiple R-squared design lie above the true value of zero, despite satisfying the width target."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (id in c(1L, 5L)) {
  sample <- trials[trials$design_id == id & trials$replication <= 60L, ]
  truth <- results$truth[results$id == id]
  plot(range(c(sample$lower, sample$upper, truth)), c(1, 60), type = "n",
        xlab = "Parameter value", ylab = "Study number",
        main = if (id == 1L) "Pearson correlation" else "R-squared, 20 predictors")
  abline(v = truth, lty = 2, col = "#555555")
  colors <- ifelse(sample$covered, "#176B87", "#BA5A31")
  segments(sample$lower, sample$replication, sample$upper, sample$replication,
            col = colors)
  points(sample$estimate, sample$replication, pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = colors)
}
```

## What Does a Larger Pilot Cost?

```{r sample_size_table}
knitr::kable(results[, c("id", "mean_n", "se_mean_n", "median_n", "p90_n",
                        "mean_width", "pct_stop_at_pilot", "pct_variance_unusable")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("ID", "Mean n", "MC SE", "Median n", "90th percentile n",
                           "Mean width", "% stop at pilot", "% unusable variance"))
```

```{r sample_size_plot, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Mean final sample sizes with Monte Carlo error bars for each design. Larger minimum pilots increase the number of observations and do not generally restore nominal coverage."}
par(mar = c(4, 21, 2, 1))
position <- rev(seq_len(nrow(results)))
plot(results$mean_n, position, xlim = c(0, max(results$mean_n + 2 * results$se_mean_n)),
      ylim = c(0.5, nrow(results) + 0.5), pch = 19, col = color,
      yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "Mean final sample size")
axis(2, at = position, labels = labels, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.75)
segments(results$mean_n - 1.96 * results$se_mean_n, position,
          results$mean_n + 1.96 * results$se_mean_n, position, col = color, lwd = 2)
```

For Pearson correlation, a larger pilot can reduce early stopping based
on an unstable variance estimate. For multiple R-squared, increasing the
pilot does not remove all difficulties: the estimate is biased upward,
and the normal-theory Wald interval has particularly poor behavior at
the boundary where the population R-squared is zero. These comparisons
must be read as operating characteristics of the published procedures,
not as a claim that any one pilot makes them reliable in general.

In the baseline null R-squared condition,
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", results$pct_stop_at_pilot[5])` of studies stopped at
the first check, with only `r results$pilot[5]` observations for twenty
predictors. The resulting upward sample R-squared values explain the
cluster of intervals far above zero in the individual-study figure.

## Why the Null Boundary Needs a Different Interval

The null R-squared condition has a further problem: increasing the sample
size does not make the usual Wald approximation correctly calibrated.
With independent normal predictors and response, at a fixed sample size

```{r null-distribution, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat("$$R^2 \\sim \\operatorname{Beta}\\left(\\frac{p}{2},",
    "\\frac{n-p-1}{2}\\right).$$", sep = "")
```

The Wald interval includes the true value zero only when
`n * R2 <= 4 * z^2 * (1 - R2)^2`. The following coverage probabilities use
that exact distribution; they have no Monte Carlo error.

```{r null_boundary}
n_fixed <- c(27, 69, 100, 400, 1000, 10000)
z <- stats::qnorm(0.975)
k <- 4 * z^2 / n_fixed
cutoff <- 2 * k / (1 + 2 * k + sqrt(1 + 4 * k))
knitr::kable(data.frame(n = n_fixed,
                        coverage = stats::pbeta(cutoff, 10, (n_fixed - 21) / 2)),
             digits = 5, row.names = FALSE)
```

As n grows, `n * R2` approaches a chi squared distribution with 20 degrees
of freedom. Consequently, fixed sample Wald coverage approaches
`Pr(chi_squared_20 <= 4 * z^2)`, or
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats::pchisq(4 * z^2, 20))`.
This fixed sample limit is different from the coverage at a random
sequential stopping point. It demonstrates that the null boundary needs
a different interval construction; an ever larger minimum pilot cannot
establish the nominal 95% coverage of this Wald interval.

For this particular null design, one can also rule out 95% coverage at
**every legal fixed sample size**, rather than relying only on the limit.
Put `c = 4 * z^2`. The inclusion event requires `R2 <= c/n`.
The beta distribution has mean `p/(n-1)` and variance
`2*p*(n-p-1)/((n-1)^2*(n+1))`. Since `p = 20 > c`, a one sided variance
inequality bounds coverage by `40/(40+(20-c)^2)`, or 65.07%, for every
`n > 21`. This loose bound is already below 95%; the exact probabilities
in the table are much smaller. It is a conclusion about fixed sampling
with the current Wald interval, not a bound for arbitrary sequential rules.

## Sample Sizes With a Different Interval Construction

An adequate sample size depends on the interval and the criterion. The
next comparison requires a full interval width no larger than the target
for every possible observed estimate, together with at least 95% coverage
under the normal model. It uses fixed sampling and intervals obtained by
inverting the finite sample distribution, rather than the package's Wald
intervals. These are reference calculations, not new exported procedures
or minimum pilot recommendations for the existing stopping rules.

For Pearson correlation, the sample correlation distribution is integrated
under bivariate normality. For multiple R-squared with random normal
predictors, the distribution is the negative binomial mixture of beta
distributions in Oliveira and Ferreira (2022), Equation 2.3. Each central
interval inverts the 0.025 and 0.975 cumulative probabilities, restricting
multiple R-squared limits to [0, 1]. At the null boundary that construction
has conservative 97.5% coverage. The width is maximized over observed
estimates; the R-squared maximization is numerical, with an independent
profile and bounds on the remaining tails.

```{r normal-reference}
tab <- reference$summary
tab$G <- format(tab$G, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
knitr::kable(tab[, c("parameter", "n", "target_width", "maximum_width", "G",
                     "coverage", "mc_lower", "mc_upper")],
             digits = 5, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Normal model", "Fixed n", "Target width",
                           "Maximum width", "Studies", "Coverage",
                           "MC lower", "MC upper"))
```

The Pearson maximum width is 0.40125 at n = 95 and 0.39917 at n = 96.
For multiple R-squared with 20 predictors, the numerical maximum is
0.30018 at n = 127 and 0.29870 at n = 128. Thus n = 96 and n = 128 meet
these width targets with the reference intervals. Independent normal data
confirm their coverage; the Monte Carlo uncertainty is shown in the table.
The script `data-raw/normal_reference.R` reproduces these results, including
the numerical distribution functions, controls, seeds, and width profiles.
The saved results are in `inst/extdata/normal_reference.rds`.

These observations do not imply that the package's Pearson interval is
adequate at n = 96, or that its null R-squared Wald interval is repaired
at n = 128. The interval construction matters. They also do not establish
performance under other data distributions or at a sequential stopping
point. A criterion allowing the width target to fail in some studies
would give different sample size requirements.

## Planning a Study

Check a design before collecting data. Start with the sensitivity
function appropriate to the parameter, using plausible population values
and assumptions. Compare wider and narrower targets and larger pilots,
then inspect coverage, sample size, and the percentage of capped studies
together. A simulation with normal data does not establish behavior for
heavy tailed or discrete data.

```{r a-small-planning-run}
seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(0.8, width = 0.4, m_0 = 50, G = 20, seed = 113)
```

Twenty studies make a quick demonstration; use thousands for a decision
about a design. Report the Monte Carlo error. If the planned procedure
does not attain adequate coverage under plausible conditions, choose a
different inferential design rather than interpreting its width target
as a confidence guarantee.

## References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy
in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients.
*Psychological Methods, 24*(4), 492-515. <https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000203>

Oliveira, I. R. C., & Ferreira, D. F. (2022). Computing the noncentrality
parameter to the distribution of the square of the sample multiple
correlation coefficient. *Chilean Journal of Statistics, 13*(2), 187-199.
<https://www.soche.cl/chjs/volumes/13/ChJS-13-02-04.pdf>
